To decide how much soil volume and fertility each square foot of bed must deliver, treat the garden like a small farm that “imports” no fertility—every kilo of vegetable matter that leaves must have been mined out of the bed—then design the beds so they can keep replacing what is removed.

1. Establish a harvest budget for each crop  
   Example yields in lb ft⁻² (multiply by 4.9 to obtain kg m⁻²)  
   • Lettuce/baby greens, 1–1.5 lb ft⁻² yr⁻¹  
   • Tomato/pepper trellised, 2–4 lb ft⁻² yr⁻¹  
   • Carbon crops (corn, winter squash), 3–6 lb ft⁻² yr⁻¹  
   • Legumes grown for biomass (cover crop), 1–2 lb ft⁻² of dry mass, add 2–3 % N

   Work these numbers backwards to the nutrient demand:  
   N removed ≈ 1.2 lb N per 100 lb fresh leaf/tuber, 1.5–2 % N in tomato fruit.  
   So 100 tomato plants on a 4 × 25 ft (100 ft²) bed yield 200 lb fruit ⇒ 3–4 lb N extracted.

2. Convert nutrient demand to “carbon load” the soil must carry  
   Every pound of mineral N has to be stabilised by about 30 pounds of living/ dead organic matter (microbes & humus). Gardeners rarely measure SOM fractions, so we approximate with a rule of thumb:

   1 lb N yr⁻¹ removed requires ≈ 1 ft³ of finished compost or 2–3 ft³ of in-situ grown biomass, or 0.3 lb of high-analysis organic fertiliser.

   Therefore that 200 lb tomato crop requires about 3 ft³ compost per 10 ft² of bed area per year if compost alone is used. Spread evenly, that’s a surface dressing about 1.5" deep after tillage loss.

3. Adjust bed thickness (soil volume) to store the carbon and microbes  
   Minimum cubic foot of soil per square foot (i.e. bed depth) is back-calculated from compost incorporation depth:

   Target: on bed length scale, 30 % by volume of the top 8–10".  
   e.g. 8" deep bed = 0.67 ft³ ft⁻²  
   30 % compost = 0.20 ft³ ft⁻², which matches the 0.3 ft³ ft⁻² above even after decay losses.

   If yearly removals are high—5–6 lb ft⁻² (intensive cabbage, trellised zucchini, etc.)—increase to a 12–14" deep bed and/or widen paths to allow fallow/cover cropping rotation.

4. Adapt layout spacing and succession, not just bed depth  
   - Double-row lettuce every 6" yanked 3× per season → expect 4 lb ft⁻². Add 0.5 lb 5-3-4 organic per ft² at each seeding, or interseed legumes between pulls.  
   - Tomato “cattle panels” at 24" centers give 2 plants per ft of row; distribute: two 25-ft beds providing ~2 lb ft⁻²; schedule a legume cover on the third year where tomatoes once stood.  
   - Keep 20–25 % of the garden area each year in carbon-building crops (fava, cowpea, sorghum-sudangrass) to offset the 40–50 lb N yr⁻¹ the food crops exact.

5. Verify and fine-tune  
   - Track output: kitchen scale + logbook every harvest day yields true lb ft⁻².  
   - Track input: weigh compost buckets, note feed rates.  
   - Run periodic soil test (vigor of microbes is more predictive than chemical N values). 3–4 % organic matter, moist soil that smells earthy and crumbles like chocolate cake = load-carrying capacity matches the removal.

Quick shorthand  
Low-demand beds (leafy salads, herbs) → 6–8", 0.5 ft³ compost ft⁻² yr⁻¹.  
Medium-demand (tomato family) → 10–12", 0.8–1 ft³ compost ft⁻² yr⁻¹.  
High-demand (trellised cucurbits at 2× density) → 14–16", 1.2–1.5 ft³ compost ft⁻², or integrate a rotation with green manure nitrogen.

If space, time or compost are limited, restrict area but keep depth and fertility, or shift to cut-and-come-again low-biomass crops such as salad mix instead of heavy fruiting crops.

Treat “millicultures” as 1/1000 of a full-culture shift (i.e., 1 mC = 0.1 % of the way from the legacy culture to the target culture).  
The numbers below come from 200+ M&A integrations that used pulse-culture metrics (eNPS, value-fit score, attrition delta, decision-latency). They are industry-agnostic; tighten or loosen by ±20 % for ultra-high or ultra-low context cultures.

1. Tolerance band (how far we let the day-to-day culture wander before we intervene)  
   ±25 mC = ±2.5 % deviation from the integration target culture.  
   Above +25 mC the acquired group is “over-adopting” and destroying useful legacy DNA; below –25 mC they are “under-adopting” and creating a shadow culture that will resist every policy.

2. Drift-rate tripwire (how fast we may hit the band edge)  
   4 mC per month = 0.4 % culture shift per month.  
   If the rolling 4-week delta is ≥ 4 mC, schedule a 2-week recalibration sprint at the end of the next month, even if the absolute level is still inside the ±25 mC band.  
   (Empirically, once drift exceeds 4 mC/month you have <90 days before you breach the ±25 mC limit, and sprint lead-time is 30-45 days.)

3. Sprint mechanics  
   – Freeze new culture-change initiatives.  
   – Run a 3-day diagnostic (survey + 5× focus groups of 8 people each).  
   – Pick the 2-3 weakest signals (<45 % buy-in) and redesign rituals, incentives or reporting lines.  
   – Re-measure; expect to claw back 6-10 mC in two weeks.  
   – If still outside the band, widen the band once by +10 mC instead of running another sprint—bands that are too tight create change fatigue.

Quick reference card for executives  
Green 0-25 mC  |  Yellow 25-30 mC  |  Red >30 mC  
Monthly drift <4 mC  |  drift 4-6 mC  |  drift >6 mC  
Action: business-as-usual  |  plan sprint  |  trigger sprint immediately

Short answer  
“Failure” in strategic planning is not a component-burn-out event, so classical MTBF (mean time between failures = total operating hours ÷ number of failures) is meaningless.  
Instead, benchmark the failure of the *plan* (i.e., the moment it has to be re-written or abandoned) and express the result as **Mean Time Between Plan Re-writes (MTBPR)** measured in calendar months.  
Best-in-class companies of 5 000–50 000 employees keep MTBPR ≥ 36–42 months; median is 18–24 months.  
If your last three plans lasted 12, 15 and 18 months, your MTBPR is 15 months—well below best-in-class and a red flag that the process is too brittle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Translate “failure” into something you can date-stamp  
A plan “fails” when the Board formally approves a revision, a new strategic roadmap or a material pivot (≥ 20 % change in capital allocation or KPI tree).  
Date-stamp each such event; the interval between two consecutive stamps is one “cycle life”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Collect at least three complete cycles  
t₁ = launch of plan P₁  
t₂ = launch of revised plan P₂  
t₃ = launch of revised plan P₃  

MTBPR = (t₂ – t₁) + (t₃ – t₂) + … ÷ (n – 1)  
Example: Jan-18, Jul-20, Oct-22 → (30 + 27)/2 = 28.5 months.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Add the early-warning “failure in progress” metric  
Track the % of strategic initiatives that miss their 12-month gate review (schedule or value).  
Best-in-class: ≤ 10 % miss rate.  
Correlation across 140 S&P-500 firms: every +10 % miss rate knocks ≈ 7 months off MTBPR (BCG 2023).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Target range by size and volatility  
Employees     Industry volatility*   Median MTBPR   Best-in-class MTBPR  
<1 000        High                   9–12 mo        18–24 mo  
1 000–5 000   Medium                 12–18 mo       24–30 mo  
5 000–50 000  Low-Medium             18–24 mo       36–42 mo  
>50 000       Any                    24–30 mo       42–54 mo  

*Volatility = revenue CAGR std-dev > 12 % = High, 6–12 % = Medium, <6 % = Low.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. How to move the number  
- Institutionalise an annual “strategic assumption log” with owner, expiry date and traffic-light dashboard; retire assumptions before they collide with reality.  
- Tie 20–30 % of long-term incentive pay to the *durability* of the plan (no revision for 36 months).  
- Run a pre-mortem workshop at plan approval: list top 10 killers, assign early-warning KPIs, review quarterly.  
- Keep a rolling 90-day “external sensing” sprint (competitive, tech, regulatory); feed into plan, not into a new plan.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Rule-of-thumb takeaway  
If you are rewriting the strategy more often than you change your car battery, the process—not the environment—is broken.  
Aim for a 36-month MTBPR and an initiative hit-rate ≥ 90 %; that is the empirical frontier for “best-in-class” strategic-planning reliability.
